lines.say: Chapter two. The call.

A federal affidavit, filed in New Jersey in early November, describes how it starts. A victim gets a call. Caller I.D. shows a local sheriff's department, the U.S. Marshals Service, or another law enforcement agency.
lines.show: A federal affidavit, filed in New Jersey in early November, describes how it starts. A victim gets a call. Caller ID shows a local sheriff's department, the U.S. Marshals Service, or another law enforcement agency.

scene.title: The call
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: The caller gives a name and a badge number, and says the victim failed to appear for jury duty. The affidavit says callers often claim a warrant has been issued, and that scammers often follow scripts. It reproduces a portion of one, handwritten, and says the Georgia Department of Corrections obtained it in a search of an inmate's cell.

scene.title: A script used by an inmate
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: Victims are then emailed or texted counterfeit arrest warrants and other official-looking documents, the affidavit says. It calls them bogus, and says they are sent to make the threats seem real.

scene.title: A counterfeit arrest warrant
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: Then the pressure. Victims are told to stay on the phone. They are told there is a gag order, and that they cannot tell family, friends or bank tellers. The affidavit says some victims reported calls that lasted more than a day.

scene.label: Source: The National Desk · report on the DOJ announcement · Nov 2026
Source: CBS19 · DOJ and the Georgia jury duty scheme · Nov 2026

lines.say: How common is it? The affidavit cites the Federal Trade Commission. More than thirty thousand complaints about jury duty impostors from January twenty twenty-one through October twenty twenty-six, with reported losses above forty million dollars. In the first ten months of this year, about eleven thousand victims reported losing around thirteen million.
lines.show: How common is it? The affidavit cites the Federal Trade Commission. More than 30,000 complaints about jury duty impostors from January 2021 through October 2026, with reported losses above $40 million. In the first ten months of this year, about 11,000 victims reported losing around $13 million.

scene.title: Jury duty impostor complaints
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: The inspector who wrote the affidavit says victims often blame themselves, and are too embarrassed or ashamed to report. The inspector says that results in widespread underreporting.

Source: KRCR News Channel 7 · Georgia inmates accused of jury duty scam · Nov 2026

lines.say: Chapter three. The payment.
Scammers then offer a way out. A bond, which they falsely promise will be refunded. Victims, the affidavit says, typically pay thousands of dollars, and some pay hundreds of thousands.

scene.title: The payment
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: The affidavit says scammers frequently direct victims to pay at a cryptocurrency ATM. First the victim withdraws cash at a bank. The affidavit says victims are coached either to say nothing to the teller about why, or to lie about the reason.

scene.label: Source: Eyewitness News ABC7NY · FBI warning on bitcoin ATM scams (file footage) · Dec 2025
Source: WTOV News 9 · sheriff warns of jury duty scam (file footage) · Apr 2026

lines.say: The affidavit says the victim then deposits the cash into a crypto kiosk and scans a QR code that the scammer sends, and the money becomes cryptocurrency, delivered to an address the scammer controls.

scene.label: Source: Eyewitness News ABC7NY · FBI warning on bitcoin ATM scams (file footage) · Dec 2025
Source: WBAY · sheriff's office warns of jury duty scam (file footage) · Aug 2026

lines.say: The affidavit includes a tracing graph. One victim's deposit hops across numerous crypto addresses in quick succession before reaching its destination. The postal inspector says that rapid movement is evidence of money laundering.

scene.title: Tracing one victim's deposit
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: Chapter four. The fake courts.

The affidavit asks a judge to seize three websites. Ejuror courts dot org. Judicial services dot org. And civil services division dot org. It says victims reported being sent there to verify their information, and some typed in Social Security numbers and birth dates.
lines.show: The affidavit asks a judge to seize three websites. ejurorcourts.org. judicialservices.org. And civilservicesdivision.org. It says victims reported being sent there to verify their information, and some typed in Social Security numbers and birth dates.

scene.title: The three target websites
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: The affidavit says the sites imitate the real U.S. Courts website, down to the fonts, the layout and the logo. On November second, a representative of the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts confirmed to an investigator that they are not official court sites.

scene.title: Real site and imitations
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: One detail. Official government sites carry a banner. It reads, quote, A dot gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. On the three sites, the postal inspector says, the banner reads, A dot gov or dot org website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Only dot gov is official.
lines.show: One detail. Official government sites carry a banner. It reads, “A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.” On the three sites, the postal inspector says, the banner reads, “A .gov or .org website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.” Only .gov is official.

scene.title: The altered banner
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: And a chat window opens in the corner. The affidavit quotes the greeting.

scene.q: Hi I'm the duty officer today. How can I assist you?
scene.case: Chat window on all three sites

lines.say: The affidavit also points to a fourth site, walkthaduck dot com. It says the three court-imitation sites load, or try to load, content from it and share its I.P. address, and that the inspector believes whoever controls it is associated with them. It says one victim paid by card through a page on that site, to an account she labeled walkthaduck.

lines.say: The site's own pages, quoted in the affidavit, call it an awareness campaign, art, social commentary and cybersecurity education. Its terms of service say, quote, We are not the government. We are not the cops. They also say, We do not operate as scammers. The inspector writes that the operators appear to be integral to jury duty fraud, which the site's operators deny.

scene.q: We are not the government. We are not the cops.

lines.say: The affidavit says webpages associated with walkthaduck dot com, including one called civiljuryservices dot org, have been the subject of more than one hundred victim complaints. Understand what this document is. It is a request to seize three web hosting accounts. It is not an indictment, and it charges no one.

lines.say: Chapter five. Behind the walls.

Who is on the other end of the line? The affidavit's author writes that, based on evidence from financial institutions, announced charges and experience, the author believes the vast majority of jury duty fraud perpetrators are inmates in the Georgia state prison system. That is a belief, not a court finding.

scene.title: Who makes the calls
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: The affidavit cites records from Bitcoin Depot, a crypto ATM company. Between September twenty twenty-two and May twenty twenty-six, victims reported losing more than nineteen million dollars to jury duty fraud there. More than forty percent of those complainants paid money mules located in Georgia.
lines.show: The affidavit cites records from Bitcoin Depot, a crypto ATM company. Between September 2022 and May 2026, victims reported losing more than $19 million to jury duty fraud there. More than 40 percent of those complainants paid money mules located in Georgia.

scene.title: Where the money went
scene.src: Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, D.N.J. Mag. No. 26-8230 (JSA), Doc. 1, filed Nov 5, 2026

lines.say: How does an inmate get a phone? The affidavit says Georgia inmates bribe prison employees, and use drones, to smuggle in cell phones, cash and drugs.

Source: CNN · the hunt for drones inside prisons (file footage) · May 2026

lines.say: From twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-three, the affidavit says, at least three hundred sixty Georgia corrections employees were arrested for smuggling contraband into state prisons.
lines.show: From 2018 to 2023, the affidavit says, at least 360 Georgia corrections employees were arrested for smuggling contraband into state prisons.

lines.say: With a phone, the affidavit says, a scammer can find victims with people-search apps, borrow a local sheriff's number with a spoofing app, and open the email, crypto and ATM accounts to collect the money.

lines.say: Then, the affidavit says, they send money to relatives and friends, buy expensive jewelry or drugs, or have a drone or a prison guard smuggle cash back inside. It says scammers are frequently members of national gangs, and that flaunting the money brings status.

lines.say: Chapter six. The government closes in.

The department's list also includes an October sentencing. On October sixteenth, two Georgia inmates who, the department says, extorted at least one hundred nineteen people over supposed missed jury duty fines were sentenced. One got two hundred months in prison. The other, one hundred twenty.
